doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Segregation and the aluminum plant in Badin
summary: Badin was segregated but blacks and whites worked together in the dangerous, hot aluminum plant.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Now, socially, what was Badin, North Carolina like in the 1930s when you were growing?
Was it segregated? Well, it was the South.
But was it a bad town, were there ways...

No, it was segregated. It wasn’t a bad town because all of them worked together. Blacks and whites worked together in the aluminum plant. 220 degrees Fahrenheit. They used to wear these suits like space suits, and sometimes that ore would pop out and get on that suit, go right through the suit and right to their arms. It was a tough job. What they did, they separated the bauxite from... They got the bauxite from South Africa, and they’d process it and get the aluminum out of there, and it would flow out into some vats. It was a tough job.
